image_description:
1. **Chart type**: Dumbbell chart (connected dot plot / slope-style comparison chart).

2. **Layout techniques**:
- Single-panel chart
- Horizontal category layout by product type
- Two dots per category connected by a light gray line
- Color used to distinguish the two comparison groups
- No faceting or small multiples
- Not stacked

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Product category (Coffee; Household cleaning products; Snacks; Candy and chewing gum; Household paper products) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Change in price (%) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Adjustment status / comparison group (“Not accounting for size” vs “Accounting for size”) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of dots; top text labels indicating color meaning |
| Time period (January 2019 to October 2023) | Temporal | Shown in title/context, applying to all plotted values |

Overall, prices have increased, suggesting potential shrinkflation. The varying rates of price increases raise questions about underlying factors. These changes significantly impact budgets, especially when wages don't keep pace with inflation. Higher price increases after accounting for size indicate consumers may be getting less value for their money, which disproportionately affects lower-income households with limited disposable income.

The time period accounts for the time before COVID-19 to after the start of the Ukraine v. comments.raw_comment: This graph examines the effects of inflation, especially after the global pandemic that occurred in 2020. The graph shows how much more expensive items were at the end of 2023 as compared to the beginning of 2019. A lot of this price change is due to the COVID-19 pandemic which led to a lot of scarcity and overshopping from people across the globe. I think an important piece of evidence to support this is the most inflated item is household paper items, the things that were most in demand during the pandemic (toilet paper, paper towels, tissues, etc). I think this graph is focused on the United States because its source is the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a US government branch. I also was interested in the accounting for size portion of this graph, because my family and I always notice how products seem to be getting smaller while prices stay the same, or even grow. This graph is proof of our experience. I would title this graph: "More Bang For Your Buck? Not in 2023!"

I wonder how COVID-19 has played a role in the outcomes of this graph. Causing a shortage of certain products led to inflation, with a big demand and low supply. This impacts my community because the items listed are sometimes used everyday. But with prices dramatically increasing, necessities are less accessible. However, the inflated economy can lead to people cutting back. People may choose to save money by using cloth towels, rather than frequently buy overpriced paper towels. This would, consequently, benefit the environment. I would title this graph: “The Prices of Products Rise.”

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, it measures how the prices and sizes of certain products are changing from the time frame January 2019 - October 2023. I noticed that the product that had the greatest increase in price was household paper products between a 30%-35% increase. I also noticed that household paper products had the greatest difference in price change when comparing the increase when not accounting for size and accounting for size. I wonder if this difference is because more people buy household paper products in bulk so the price would be significantly higher when accounting for size than not. However, I noticed that coffee has the smallest increase in price at only about 20%-23% and also the smallest difference between the price increase when accounting for size and not accounting for size. Compared to household paper products, I think that there is a smaller disparity between price increases because people are less likely to buy coffee in bulk, so it does not make as much of a difference in price increase whether the size is accounted for or not. Overall, there is a trend of price increases for each object, representing inflation, and I wonder if since the data is from 2019-2023 if this inflation is a result of the COVID pandemic. This relates to my community because prices of objects in supermarkets keep rising and it makes certain necessities less accessible to people. My headline for this graph would be: “Prices, Objects, Inflation, Oh My!”.

This graph displays the change in price of products such as coffee, house cleaning products, snacks, candy/chewing gum, and household paper products from January 2019 to October 2023. It shows the change in price accounting for size and not accounting for size. I notice that the price of every product on this graph has gone up more than 20% since 2019 with or without accounting for weight. I can conclude this is likely due to rising inflation. Although coffee has increased the least in price out of all the products listed, the price has still increased significantly and it is noticeable. I constantly hear my dad complaining about coffee prices. Additionally, the price of snacks and candy at my school has gone up 50 cents in this past year. This makes me less likely to want to buy snacks from school because I would rather save my money and not buy expensive snacks/candy. I wonder if this is true for the global market. Are sales of these items declining because of how inflated the prices are?

comments.raw_comment:
This graph depicts the rise in prices for common grocery items, such as snacks or cleaning products, from January 2019 to October 2023. The graph accounts for with and without size/weight of each item. All of these items have surpassed a 20% increase. Household paper products, when accounting for size, have the largest increase on this graph with a surge of 35%. The smallest price increase, which is just over 20%, is coffee (not accounting for size). What stuck out to me the most is that candy and gum, when accounting for size, have an almost 30% increase as compared to cleaning products with less than a 25% increase. I wonder why candy increased more than other products. I wonder what this graph would look like if more items. For example, if meats, bread, and dairy were accounted for. Would they have price increases too? I also wonder if this graph would be affected by data from November 2023 to now. Would there be any significant changes? This affects my community because the price of living increases with every year. As a student entering college soon, having to worry about college expenses as well as everyday things I may need, such as food and cleaning supplies, will be difficult. Both expenses are becoming more expensive every day. All students my age are worried about affordability as we take our next steps into adulthood. Will we be able to live in a world where buying gum is becoming too expensive?

“Are These Prices Eating You? Food Prices Jump Since January 2019”

I wonder why the price of household paper products has increased. During the pandemic, many people were obsessed with the toilet paper shortage, increasing demand. I wonder if this demand led manufacturers to increase prices. I also wonder if environmental factors, such as lumber shortages, affects the price of paper. I wonder if the change in price accounting for size is larger than not accounting for size because less product is being sold. I am curious if the trend of increased prices is also caused by inflation.

This affects me an my community because we purchase these goods at inflated prices. Paper and household cleaning products are perhaps the most functional, but all can be enjoyed day-to-day. People may have to limit their superfluous purchases (such as candy and snacks) in the future if prices continue to rise.

I wonder what the future of our country is and if we will go into a recession because of this. - this graph displays the changing prices of different consumer goods. In the 4-year range, the prices jumped within a 20%-35% window. It is evident that paper products had the highest jump, with food and cleaning products using paper having the highest. I wonder why paper has had such an inflation in price. It is one of the most used products, so it is both interesting and worrying that it would be so much more expensive. On the other hand, there has been a surprisingly low jump in price for other cleaning products. It leads me to wonder why only paper cleaning products are being so affected by inflation. This affects every community because of how important paper is to standard life. Not only paper products, but food packaging and household products use paper. If such a general material has had such an upsurge if price, it will cause many other aspects of life to be expensive and possibly unaffordable for some. 
A possible title: “If money is paper, why do we need to spend more money on paper?”

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the graph presents a comparison of the change in prices for common grocery items that have gone up over four years (from January 2019 to October 2023), both with and without accounting for the size. I wonder if when accounting for size, the increased cost shows a pattern that the price remains the same or increases while the product size decreases. Furthermore, what are the reasons behind this trend; are there economic factors or changes in manufacturing costs? Are these possible issues representative of a broader trend in the market of groceries? This highly impacts my community and I because most students have budgets or work to be able to afford to get a university education. This means we all have to budget more carefully if the amount of product is shrinking but pricing is rising since we are getting less food/necessities for our money. This could make a big difference in some people’s quality of life. A catchy headline that captures what’s going on in this graph is "Secret Shrinkage: Tracking Hidden Risings in Grocery Bills".

I notice from this graph that all five popular grocery items displayed have increased in price by atleast 20% from 2019 to 2023. The item with the greatest increase is household paper products at around 31-35% and the item with the smallest increase listed is coffee at around 21-23%. It also appears that for each of the 5 items, the difference in price increase when adjusting for size and not adjusting for size is atleast around 2%. 

From evaluating this graph, I wonder what causes the difference in price when evaluating for size for each of these items. Have many manufacturers decreased item sizes over time for cost cutting measures, and is this what causes the price increase accounting for size to be more substantial. I also wonder if there are other trends or explanations for the "accounting for size" increase always being greater. Does this also mean that the average product size for each of the items listed has decreased over the last 4 years? 

This has a tremendous impact on myself and my community being that increases of over 20% for all of these items certain affects an individuals purchasing power and could limit how accessible these items are to various people. Additionally, if item quantities have shrunk which could be evident by the "accounting for size" variable, then individuals may be forced to purchase more of a certain item  or make more frequent purchases.

"Price Changes to Everyday Items"

The first thing you notice when you look at the graph is the fact that every grocery item increased in price over the 4 years, each over at least 20%. The biggest increase being in household paper products and the least being coffee. Obviously the biggest world wide event to happen in this time period is the pandemic. I also wonder where they pulled this data, specifically what countries. The pandemic affected parts of the world differently, so based on where the data was pulled could definitely affect the results of the data and to what population we can associate it to. 
I would imagine that products like paper towels, toilet paper, and tissues, products that are usually associated with sickness, are what contributed to the price increase of household paper products. As demand increases, so does the price. It also makes sense for coffee to have the smallest increase as people were likely less active during the pandemic and so then did the need for coffee. This also most likely shows the average rate of inflation. 
I think that it's really interesting that during this 4 year span, I never noticed that prices were increasing, let alone by 25%. I think it's important to be aware of these price changes and to keep track of how fast or slow products rise in price in order to accurately busget yourself. A title I wold give this graph is "Everyday use, everyday increase"

Knowing how prices of products have changed can help inform large scale wage changes on local, state, and federal level. In order for wages to be adjusted in a way that properly reflects the cost of everyday life, you need to have a complete knowledge of the factors going into that cost.

comments.raw_comment: One big thing that I noticed in this graph of price change is that the prices of various every day products from January 2019 to October 2023 are consistently higher when accounting for size than when not accounting for size. Another thing that I noticed is that in just under 5 years, the prices of all of these products has increased quite significantly- all of the products have increased anywhere from 20% to about 35% from their previous price almost 5 years earlier. I wonder how this trend in increased prices will increase over the course of the next five years. Will we see a similar increase in the price inflation, or will it increase exponentially? It is scary to think about how the trend over time shows that there is a concurrent increase in prices and decrease in the size of the product that you are buying. I wonder how prices overall will look in the near future. This issue directly relates to me and my community. As a constant participant in the world of consumerism, I find myself buying something almost every day, whether it be a living necessity or something for my own enjoyment. More importantly, as a college student with limited personal income, the general inflation of prices has proven to be detrimental to my wallet, as I am spending more money to receive less product. A catchy headline for this graph could possibly be "Prices Up, Quantities Down- The Rollercoaster of Product Inflation".

comments.raw_comment: The graph are results from January 2019 to October 2023, and the choices they picked for the products were products such that every single American could have bought at least one of these items during that time. Paper products have the greatest price increase when accounting for size. "Accounting for size" adjusts the price change to reflect any changes in the quantity or size of the product, which is leading to an even higher price per dollar value than from years past. I wonder what caused the increase in prices and whether it was due to inflation, increased production costs or just pure greed. What do you notice?

I've noticed that the prices of the five common grocery items have increased by at least 20% in the last four years, with the smallest increase seen in coffee and the largest in household paper products. Along with having the highest increase when size is not accounted for, household paper products also achieved a higher rate of increase when size is accounted for.

- How does this relate to you and your community?

As a student, it is important to understand inflation as we are starting to learn to budget. Understanding the causes of inflation and its consequences will help us with long-term financial planning.

- Catchy headline

2. This makes me really curious about how more perishable grocery items have increased in price or decreased in size, based on what we are observing with more shelf stable items. It also makes me wonder how these changes in quantity/size impact overall cost of living.
3. As college students, these questions are especially relevant. For those of us getting by with grants and scholarships, we have a fixed amount of money each term that has to cover tuition, books, and our living expenses. When we have to pay more for the same quantity, or the same for a smaller quantity of a necessary item, our money doesn’t take us as far, necessitating part time work at the expense of internships or research. 
4. Based on this, I think that “Size Matters: Unpacking Grocery Store Price Hikes” would be an apt title.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph is a comparison of price changes for various consumer goods from January 2019 to October 2023, specifically for coffee, household cleaning products, snacks, candy and chewing gum, and household paper products. It compares the price changes when not accounting for size and when accounting for size. The prices for all the items seems to have increased over the period. This suggests that there may have been a reduction in the size of the products, a phenomenon known as shrinkflation. I wonder about the changes in different rates of price increase between the goods. It would be interesting to investigate the factors contributing. There are a lot of impacts on the community and me as price increases in everyday consumer goods have a significant impact on budgets, especially when wages do not increase together with inflation. The higher rates of increase when accounting for size can show how the consumers might be getting less value for their money over time, which makes it harder to buy most goods. For communities, this can lead to disproportionately affect lower-income households even more severely as they do not have the luxury of disposable income.

Catchy headline:
"Feeling Robbed?"

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I noticed was how much each product’s price change increased when accounting for quantity and size, nodding to how companies are increasing prices because of inflation but also decreasing the quantity/volume of products to reach desirable profit margins. Given that consumers purchase these products very often, it is probably difficult to notice subtle changes in quantity especially over long periods. I wonder whether this trend applies to all other consumer items since there could be other items that may not be as different when, for example, adjusting for size or increasing prices due to inflation. I also wonder how household paper products' largest change in price relates to COVID-19 when many households stocked up on toilet paper to the point where stores ran out of paper products. I wonder if these household paper product companies noticed how crucial their products are to consumers and decided to increase profit margins even greater than they were before. This relates to me both as a consumer and a statistician because, in an economy already struggling with inflation, shrinkflation, COVID-19 recovery, etc., it is difficult to navigate what products are worth my time and money. To see these companies increasing their profit margins makes me question whether they have their consumers’ best interests in mind or solely want to exploit us for money. A catchy headline could be “Pockets Feeling Lighter? Higher Prices and Lesser Quantities Could Explain Why.”

comments.raw_comment:
The first thing I noticed is the scale of the x-axis. First of all, since the x-axis does not start at 0, the price increase of coffee seems to be small in comparison to the others, even though a 20% increase is still fairly large. Additionally, since the x-axis is based on percentage increases instead of actual dollar increases, it standardizes the scale so it is easier to compare the 5 items. However, this means we do not know how the dollars increased, so it can be difficult to interpret the actual difference in pricing. Since the item categories are very general, I wonder what items are included in each category, and how the prices are calculated across all those items. This information is very relevant to everyone in my community because we all went through the pandemic, so to see how most of the products being used on a daily basis have increased significantly from before coronavirus hit the US is quite important to us all. Also, as a college student, knowing how much more these items are costing motivates me to save more and reduce my spending on unnecessary items.
Title:  “Less Costs More: How Shrinkflation is Affecting Essentials Post-Pandemic”

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I notice is that the change in price from January 2019 to October 2023 is higher when you account for size than when you do not account for size. I also notice, at least for these 5 chosen items, that the minimum percentage change of price is slightly above 20% increase and the maximum being just under 35% increase. One could also see that household paper products has increased the most and coffee has increased the least. The spread of the size variability also seems fairly consistent between coffee, household cleaning products, and candy and chewing gum, being at about a difference of 2-3%. Even further we see that household paper products have the biggest spread in price change, at about a 4% difference. The main thing I wonder is whether the big price change of household paper products has to do with recent increases in environmental friendliness, that people want to use more paper products to help reduce the amount of plastic being used. I also wonder how the price of inflation has affected these items, and what other events have lead to these items having their respective price change. This relates to my community, as a college student, in that we are currently living in a high-inflation society. Where the price of inflation and prices are drastically higher than the increase of pay. A catchy headline could possibly be "Are Your Household Essentials Really Essential? – How Your Common Essentials May Become a Luxury"

comments.raw_comment:
Inflation in our nation😭

I find it evident the extent as to which prices have risen over but a three year period. It's rather troubling. The graph makes me wonder if purchasing in bulk is better in the long run for the average consumer. Perhaps buying a lot of something at one time is more a cost-efficient mean of purchasing in comparison to buying just enough to get you by over and over again. Similar to several other economists from Elk Rapids in this comment section, I, too, have noticed this inflation in my everyday life. For example, Frito Lay, the company that owns Fritos and Pepsi was put in a predicament in which they had to raise their prices to continue making the same amount of profit. Frito Lay had to raise the prices of Fritos as opposed to raising the price of Pepsi, where the real problem was because Fritos are less elastic in peoples' everyday lives and if Pepsi prices rose, they wouldn't sell as well. This sure leaves you with something to think about. 🤔

I am curious as to how sizes of household paper products are taken into account here. For example, would a small size be four paper towel rolls vs. a larger size being twelve? Also, what kinds of household paper products are included in this visualization? Toilet paper? Paper towels? Napkins? I am a college student who buys such products very frequently. Moreover, I live in a college town where fellow students like me need to have easy access to these products. If items like paper and cleaning products keep increasing in price, this would have a significant impact on accessibility of these basic yet very necessary grocery items for consumers like students who do not have a significant amount of money to spend. comments.raw_comment:
When looking at the graph I notice that for every one of the five popular grocery store items, when size is accounted for the change in price for all items goes up by a higher percentage. I also notice that this graph includes pre, mid, and post pandemic dates which would be an influence in the price fluctuations. I think that the grocery stores have found that because these are such staple household items, they can easily raise prices and cover that with size without the consumers noticing.

I wonder if the reason in the increase is due to inflation. I know these past few years inflation rates have been at an all time high and that could definitely be a reason for the price increase. I also am wondering if maybe the demand of COVID and the fact that during the pandemic most of these items were hard to come by, especially paper products, has allowed grocery stores to raise their prices without the consequence of less people buying them. And the fact that they were able to raise the prices has given them confidence to constantly keep increasing the prices of these items.

This directly applies to my community of being a student in college who does not have a full time job nor steady income. These items are ones that I know both me and many of my peers purchase almost weekly. The increase in prices makes these essential items less affordable but because of the constant demand, prices will not drop and we are forced to pay it.

Title:"Cheap Necessities: Is that so hard?"

I wonder the extent to which the public is aware of these tactics. Are most consumers cognizant of the relationship between price changes and accompanying changes in product size? I know that for me, I feel deceived after looking at this graph. I had not considered the effect of the change in size on the true change in the price of a product. I wonder if others feel similarly or if they already knew about this and accepted it. 

In my community, I believe this discussion could spark a range of insights and reflections. Discussions within the community could also delve into potential solutions or responses to these practices. Members might brainstorm ideas for promoting greater transparency in pricing or advocating for stronger consumer protections.

This can be extremely problematic if these everyday items become too unaffordable for certain communities.
